The segment that fails

CHAPTER 9 (LOLLIS) · CHAPTER 48 (TAN, KASLIWAL, FESSLER)

Three structures decide whether a lumbar segment translates: the pars, the facet joint, and the disc. Two of them are described below; the third carries the load that breaks them.

Pars interarticularis

Ch 9 places the pars as the lateral-most portion of the lamina, the piece that connects and functionally links the superior and inferior articulating processes. Without it, the stabilising effect of the facet joint below is lost.

KEY POINT — CH 9

Full-thickness violation of the pars risks spinal instability and anterolisthesis. The pars is thinner at its rostral-medial portion and thicker caudal-laterally.

Ch 15 adds the dimensions: the pars sits between pedicle, lamina, inferior articular facet and transverse process origin, resists forces in excess of 1251 N, and has a cross-sectional area of about 0.75 cm² — two cortical layers with trabecular bone between them.

Facet orientation down the lumbar spine

Lumbar facets occupy a plane between sagittal and coronal, becoming progressively coronal as you descend. Ch 9 states the surgical consequence directly: the entry into the facet joint is found progressively more laterally toward the lumbosacral junction, and the coronal orientation there is an important element in preventing spondylolisthesis.

L1–2 · 25° from sagittal → L5–S1 · 50° from sagittal

Ch 48 makes the same point from the sacral side: because of the sacrovertebral angle created by the tilt of the sacrum, the L5–S1 facet joint prevents ventral displacement of the lumbar spine on the sacrum.

Where the root actually is

The single most useful rule in Ch 9 for slip-related radiculopathy: in the thoracic and lumbar spine, nerve roots exit below their like-named pedicle, and the exiting root leaves the canal some distance above the disc. Only after it has left the bony foramen does it cross the plane of the disc.

CONSEQUENCE AT L4–5

A posterolateral L4–5 herniation sits just lateral to the PLL and compresses the shoulder of the L5 root as it begins to descend along the medial border of the L5 pedicle. A far-lateral L4–5 herniation, one to two centimetres more laterally and beyond the foramen, compresses the L4 root.

Because foraminal height is commonly two to three times its width, compression is usually a dorsal-ventral problem rather than a rostral-caudal one. Ch 9 notes that when restoring disc height helps, it is more often through the associated increase in foraminal sagittal width than through foraminal height itself.

Details worth holding on to

In a balanced spine the midportion of the C7 vertebral body sits atop the L5–S1 pivot point, located at the dorsal aspect of the L5–S1 disc. Lumbar lordosis comes principally from disc shape rather than vertebral body shape, with some reverse wedging at L4 and L5 adding to lower lumbar lordosis.

The mammillary process sits at the junction of the superior articulating process and transverse process and is an important landmark for pedicle screw insertion, though it is not visible in every patient. Following the lateral edge of the pars rostrally and slightly laterally, staying lateral to the facet capsule, exposes the superior articular process and transverse process without destabilising the supra-adjacent facet.

The ligamentum flavum is absent along the rostral half of the ventral laminar surface — relevant if you are relying on it to protect the dura. It has two layers with a virtual gliding space between them, and the outer layer is discontinuous in the midline; even in florid spondylosis a midline cleavage plane can be found and used as a safe point of entry.

Anomalies occur in over 10% of nerve roots studied, conjoined roots being more common than extradural anastomoses; consider them when radiographic and clinical findings disagree. Transitional lumbosacral vertebrae were found in 20% of 750 consecutive whole-spine MRIs (14.5% with six lumbar-type vertebrae, 5.3% with four, 0.13% with three). Use one localisation scheme across pre- and intraoperative imaging.

The medial branch of the dorsal primary ramus supplies the facet capsule, periosteum of the neural arch and dorsal ligaments, giving twigs to the joints above and below its course. The sinuvertebral nerve (nerve of Luschka) re-enters through the rostral foramen to innervate the discs above and below plus the ventral dura. Both are implicated in axial back pain.

How the slip happens

CHAPTER 15 (PORENSKY, MOHYELDIN, THOMAS, WEINSTEIN)

Spondylolisthesis is translational movement of one vertebra on another. Spondylolysis — a pars defect — is one mechanism of that translation, not a synonym for it.

Three mechanical routes to translation

Physiologic lordosis centres the trunk over the femoral heads and keeps the internal axis of rotation in line with the major force vectors, giving a short moment arm. Loss of lordosis (flat-back) or hyperflexion shifts the IAR dorsally, increasing the bending moment and converting axial load into shear across disc, pedicle, pars and facets. The usual resistors — oblique facet geometry and the erector spinae — are at a mechanical disadvantage in flexion. Stress concentrates at the caudal pedicle margin and progresses across the pars, which is weaker than the pedicle and fails. Whether by single overload or fatigue is still debated; probably both. The same mechanism prevents healing, so a fibrous nonunion results, which may allow progressive listhesis with pars elongation.

Lumbar extension also generates pars stress. The frequency of spondylolisthesis in gymnasts has been attributed to hyperextension on landing upright with accentuated lordosis: sudden deceleration of the extended spine increases shear along the disc space, which in the lower lumbar spine is angled to the line of deceleration, producing further extension, more shear and greater pars stress. The disc is less stiff in extension, making ventral translation more probable. Supporting this, asymptomatic spondylolysis has been reported in up to 50% of Scheuermann patients, who carry a compensatory lordosis.

Torque matters particularly in the degenerative type, where the pars stays intact. With degeneration the disc loses its ability to resist shear and torsion. A developmental variation toward a more vertical facet plane may potentiate degenerative anterolisthesis. Torsional stress conveyed to the caudal facet distorts the lamina-pedicle angle and leaves that facet less able to resist shear; the contralateral facet then takes more shear and may be damaged in turn.

NATURAL HISTORY — ISTHMIC

The initial slip can be marked, but progression in adulthood is unusual. Slip is more prone to progress at L4–5 than L5–S1 and may reach 28% in the teenage years; whether a given subluxation will progress is difficult to predict.

PAIN ATTRIBUTION

A Framingham Heart Study subgroup analysis found a higher prevalence of spondylolysis than previously reported (11.5% versus 6%) and no association of spondylolysis or spondylolisthesis with low back pain — the chapter's conclusion is that these lesions are not a major cause of back pain in the general population.

Ch 22 says the same thing from its own literature: most patients with a spondylolysis or isthmic spondylolisthesis are unlikely to be at risk of increased back pain symptoms. In the primary-care series it quotes, 3% of isolated back pain presentations had spondylolisthesis.

What the chapter says about treatment

Very little, and it's worth knowing the limit of the source. Treatment of each type of spondylolysis depends on the extent of neural compression and motion segment instability; decompressive laminectomy, foraminotomies, arthrodesis and internal fixation may be required. For the degenerative type: it is commonly associated with stenosis and neurogenic claudication, decompression often relieves symptoms, and fusion with internal fixation may be required where there is radiographic instability or severe back pain.

Ch 15 also gives the mechanism behind the posture dependence: flexion stretches the protruding ligamentum flavum and PLL and reduces overriding laminae and facets, increasing lateral recess, foraminal and canal dimensions, while extension aggravates them. Returning to the erect posture recompresses the roots — the shopping cart sign, and why bicycling or uphill walking is often tolerated.

OUT OF SCOPE FOR THESE FOUR CHAPTERS

Nothing in Ch 9, 15, 22 or 48 discusses the decompression-alone versus decompression-plus-fusion trials (SPORT, SLIP, Försth, NORDSTEN-DS). Any statement on that question has to come from the papers themselves, not from this page.

What the slip does to the root

CHAPTER 22 (LAVELLE, KITAB, RAMAKRISHNAN, BENZEL)

Compression is the mechanism everyone reaches for. This chapter's argument is that in a translating segment the exiting root is also stretched, and that the two roots involved fail in different ways at the same level.

Root behaviour explorer — L4–5 motion segment
SELECT A DEFORMITY STATE

Why the root can't get out of the way

The lumbar root is tethered in two places: at the neck of the nerve root sheath as it exits the dural sac, and at the lateral aspect of the foramen, where it is attached to both pedicles rostrally and caudally by the foraminal ligaments. These ligaments limit root excursion and increase in size and strength distally in the lumbar spine, and are described as equalising stresses on neural structures during movement of spine and limbs.

THE CHAPTER'S CENTRAL CLAIM

The dorsal root ganglion, with its central and peripheral components, may represent the primary focus of stretch deformation during the pathomechanical behaviour of a failing functional spinal unit. Mechanical deformation of DRG cells induces membrane changes manifesting as ectopic discharges and increased excitability, which in turn trigger chronic changes in the excitability or synaptic plasticity of dorsal horn neurons.

Anatomic facts behind that claim

  • In the foramen — the exit zone — the root occupies only 30–50% of the cross-sectional area, so there is ample room for the exiting root in the normal state.
  • The DRG most commonly sits directly beneath the foramen; the S1 DRG is the exception, usually lying inside the spinal canal.
  • If tethering occurs at two points close to the pedicle, root stretch at the area of the DRG may occur.
  • L4, L5 and S1 traverse two or more mobile segments on their longer path out, theoretically exposing them to greater risk of compression or stretch — a partial explanation for the higher incidence of pain in these roots.
  • Static lateral recess syndrome is fixed, permanent entrapment. When a segment has erratic or excessive motion, as with instability associated with a spondylolisthesis, a dynamic lateral recess syndrome may occur.

HONEST LIMIT

The chapter states plainly that the magnitude of stretch required to cause a nerve root injury producing pain or electrophysiologic dysfunction in humans remains unknown, and that animal models do not reproduce the extent of damage, the biologic milieu or the time course of axonal injury in humans. The strain thresholds above are rat data.

Perfusion

Vascular hypoperfusion is the other proposed mechanism. Intraradicular blood flow in the root of patients with a disc herniation fell while the root was compressed; intraoperative straight-leg raising showed a sharp decrease in flow at the angles where symptoms were worst, and flow improved after discectomy. The DRG has an abundant intrinsic supply — blood flow roughly twice that of the nerve root, similar to spinal cord grey matter — but the effect of quasi-static or dynamic stretch on root or DRG venous pressure, flow and blood-neural barrier function is largely unknown.

REDUCTION

Stretch-induced nerve injury is described in Ch 22 as a well-known complication of lumbosacral spondylolisthesis reduction.

Getting there

CHAPTER 48 (TAN, KASLIWAL, FESSLER)

Ch 48 is an exposure chapter, not a technique chapter. It gives the corridor, the layers, the structure that will be in the way, and the complication that follows if it is mishandled.

Exposure selector
SELECT A TARGET
ORIENTATION RULE

The L5–S1 disc space lies at the level of the interlaminar space. As you proceed rostrally each disc space becomes more rostral in relation to the interlaminar space; as a rule of thumb about half the lamina must be removed to approach L3–4 or L4–5.

Two other dorsal cautions from the chapter: dissecting laterally over the sacrum can inadvertently enter the dorsal foramina and damage the dorsal roots; and the ligamentum flavum is thinnest in the midline, made of two layers extending laterally to form the ventral portion of the facet capsule.

Traps named in the chapter

When palpating through quadratus lumborum the transverse processes can be mistaken for the vertebral bodies. If you are in the correct plane the psoas comes into view; a common mistake is to enter the retropsoas space, a blind pouch between psoas and quadratus lumborum.

The ascending iliolumbar vein crosses the L4–5 disc space and must be ligated and separated to expose that disc and the L5 body. It drains into either the vena cava or the left iliac vein and becomes a tether if the cava must be moved from left to right; avulsion directly off the cava causes rapid blood loss.

As the left iliac vein courses over the L5–S1 disc space it can be stretched and flattened. It must be identified and controlled before opening that disc space. It can also be large, bulbous and difficult to retract; if lacerated, get proximal and distal control before repair.

On the surface of the psoas the genitofemoral nerve appears as a small white structure lying on the muscle belly. Protect it — injury causes postoperative groin pain.

The plexus spans L4 to S1 and lies directly ventral to L5 and the L5–S1 disc; in males it innervates bladder, vas deferens and seminal vesicles and closes the bladder neck during ejaculation. Damage may cause retrograde ejaculation during ALIF. For exposures above L5 the plexus is retracted medially; below L5, laterally. Enter to the right of the left iliac artery and vein and sweep tissue left to right to retract it en bloc; blunt dissection, gentle retraction, minimal electrocautery.

The paraspinous sympathetic lumbar chain usually has to be stretched or cut during a ventral approach. The patient typically complains of a cold foot on the opposite side; in fact the ipsilateral foot is abnormally warm from loss of vasoconstriction on the operated side.

The plexus lies in psoas major; penetration or aggressive retraction must be avoided. The muscle is often markedly enlarged and bulging over the spine. Begin psoas dissection at the midline, at the disc space, and hold it off the field with a pin retractor once dissection is complete.

Sacral anatomy you need for lumbosacral work

The sacral articular crest carries a functional superior articular process at S1 facing rostrally and dorsally; because of the sacrovertebral angle it resists ventral displacement of the lumbar spine on the sacrum. The sacrum is the most variable part of the spine — lengthening or shortening of the lumbar spine by deletion or addition of segments is not uncommon. The dorsal root ganglia lie in the sacral canal, central and rostral to the foramina from which their rami emerge.

Conflicts and citation problems found while reading

CONFLICT 1 — DEGENERATIVE SLIP CEILING

Ch 15: degenerative subluxation "does not usually exceed 30%". Ch 22: degenerative spondylolisthesis "rarely exceeds 35% translation of the vertebrae" (citing Cauchoix, Benoist, Chassaing 1976). Same book, two figures.

CONFLICT 2 — CLASSIFICATION NAME

Ch 15 names the five-type scheme the Newman classification while citing Wiltse, Newman & Macnab 1976 for it. Most sources call this the Wiltse classification.

AGREEMENT WORTH NOTING

Ch 15 and Ch 22 agree on the two things that matter clinically at L4–5: the degenerative slip is commonest there, and it produces central plus lateral recess stenosis compressing the traversing L5 root.

Not covered by these chapters

  • Decompression alone versus decompression plus fusion — no trial data in any of the four chapters.
  • Reduction technique, instrumented reduction of high-grade slips and lumbosacral fixation — these sit in Ch 86 and Ch 89, which were read but are not represented on this page.
  • Interbody options for spondylolisthesis (PLIF/TLIF indications, fusion rates, complication rates) — Ch 80.

Say the word and any of those three can be added as a fifth panel.
